note: Non-temporal economics: structural concepts (GDP/national income theory, sectors, poverty as concept, planning framework, consumer rights, microeconomics, open economy theory). Awaiting future non-temporal economics architecture.

nodes.label: Primary Sector (Agriculture)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Activities using natural resources directly: agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry, mining. Forms the base for all other products. Was the largest producing sector in 1973 but by 2003 overtaken by tertiary sector. Still employs over 50% of India's workforce despite producing only 25% of GDP.

nodes.label: Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year. Shows how big the economy is. Measured by a central government ministry collecting data from all states and UTs. Only final goods counted to avoid double counting of intermediate goods.

nodes.label: Final Goods vs Intermediate Goods
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Final goods reach consumers directly (e.g., biscuits at Rs 60). Intermediate goods are used up in producing final goods (e.g., wheat flour at Rs 10, wheat at Rs 8). Only final goods are counted in GDP to avoid double counting -- value of intermediates already included in final goods.

nodes.label: Organised Sector
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Enterprises registered with government following laws (Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Gratuity Act). Workers get regular salary, fixed hours, overtime pay, paid leave, provident fund, medical benefits, pension. Only about 7% of India's workers are in this sector.

nodes.label: Unorganised Sector
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Small, scattered units largely outside government control. Rules exist but are not followed. Low-paid, irregular jobs with no overtime, leave, or job security. Includes casual workers, street vendors, small farmers, artisans. About 93% of India's workers. SC/ST and backward communities disproportionately represented.

nodes.label: Public Sector
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Government owns most assets and provides services. Aim is not just profit but social welfare. Examples: railways, post office, BSNL, government hospitals and schools. Government raises money through taxes to fund these activities and services.

nodes.label: Private Sector
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Ownership of assets and delivery of services by private individuals or companies. Main aim is profit. Examples: Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO), Reliance Industries, private hospitals, private schools. Activity guided by profit motive.

nodes.label: Sector Interdependence
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: All three sectors are highly interdependent. Primary provides raw materials to secondary. Secondary provides tools/machinery to primary. Tertiary (transport, trade, banking) supports both. Disruption in one affects others -- e.g., transport strike affects food supply and farmer incomes.

nodes.label: Foreign Trade
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Main historical channel connecting countries. Creates opportunity for producers to reach beyond domestic markets. Leads to integration of markets across countries: prices of similar goods tend to equalise, and producers compete across borders. Example: Chinese toys displacing Indian toys.

nodes.label: Integration of Markets
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Through foreign trade, goods move between markets, consumer choice rises, prices of similar goods tend to equalise, and producers across countries compete directly despite being thousands of miles apart. MNCs interlink production processes globally.

nodes.label: Globalisation Impact on Indian Producers
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Top Indian companies benefited: invested in newer technology, raised production standards, successful foreign collaborations. Some emerged as MNCs themselves (Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy, Asian Paints). But small producers hit hard by competition -- many units shut down, workers jobless. Small industry employs 20 million.

nodes.label: Consumer Rights
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Six rights under COPRA: right to safety, right to information, right to choice, right to redressal, right to representation, right to consumer education. Consumers are often in a weak position against sellers. Rules and regulations needed to protect against exploitation.

nodes.label: Unfair Trade Practices
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Includes: weighing less than stated, adding hidden charges, selling adulterated or defective goods, false advertising claims, not providing cash memos. Powerful companies can manipulate markets using wealth and media. Examples: powder milk falsely claimed better than mother's milk, cigarette companies denying cancer link.

nodes.label: Challenges of Consumer Redressal
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Process becoming cumbersome, expensive, and time consuming. Often requires hiring lawyers. Cash memos not always issued, making evidence gathering difficult. Most purchases are small retail sales. Laws on compensation for injury from defective products unclear. Consumer awareness spreading slowly.

nodes.label: Mixed Economy Model
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: India chose a system combining the best features of socialism and capitalism -- a socialist society with a strong public sector but also private property and democracy. The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1948 and Directive Principles of the Constitution reflected this outlook. Government would plan while encouraging private sector participation.

nodes.label: Goals of Five Year Plans
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Four main goals: Growth (increase in GDP and productive capacity), Modernisation (adoption of new technology and social change), Self-reliance (avoiding dependence on imports especially food), Equity (ensuring benefits reach poor sections, reducing inequality). These goals sometimes conflicted with each other.

nodes.label: High Yielding Variety (HYV) Seeds
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Also called 'miracle seeds', these required correct quantities of fertiliser, pesticide, and regular water supply. Only farmers with reliable irrigation and financial resources could initially benefit, causing regional and farmer-size disparities. Government subsidies later helped small farmers access these inputs.

nodes.label: Marketed Surplus
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The portion of agricultural produce sold in the market by farmers. Economist C.H. Hanumantha Rao noted that a good proportion of rice and wheat produced during green revolution was available as marketed surplus, causing food grain prices to decline relative to other goods, benefiting low-income groups.

nodes.label: Debate Over Agricultural Subsidies
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Subsidies were needed initially to encourage adoption of new HYV technology. Critics argue they should be phased out once technology is widely adopted, as they largely benefit fertiliser industry and prosperous farmers. Supporters argue farming remains risky and poor farmers cannot afford inputs without subsidies.

nodes.label: Role of Public Sector (1950-1990)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: State given commanding heights of the economy because private sector lacked capital for large investment and market was too small. Public sector built industrial base, diversified industry, and provided employment. However, many PSUs incurred huge losses, lacked competition, and it was hard to close loss-making units.

nodes.label: License Raj
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: System of excessive regulation where entrepreneurs needed government permission to start, close, or expand firms, and to decide production quantities. Often misused by large industrialists who obtained licenses to prevent competitors from entering. Led to rent-seeking, corruption, and inefficiency rather than productive enterprise.

nodes.label: Structural Change in Economy (1950-1990)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Agriculture's share in GDP fell from over 50% to 34.9% by 1990-91, while industry rose from 11.8% to 24.6% and services to 40.5%. However, 65% of population remained in agriculture by 1990 -- industrial and service sectors failed to absorb agricultural workforce. Service sector share grew peculiarly fast for a developing nation.

nodes.label: Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The market value of all goods and services produced in a country during a year. Derived from agricultural, industrial, and service sectors. A key indicator of economic growth. The GDP 'cake' analogy: growth means increasing the size of the cake so more people can benefit.

nodes.label: Self-Reliance as Planning Goal
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: First seven five year plans emphasised avoiding imports of goods that could be produced domestically, especially food. Aimed to reduce dependence on foreign countries and prevent foreign interference in India's sovereignty. Led to import substitution policy but also reduced international competitiveness.

nodes.label: Equity as Planning Goal
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Ensuring benefits of economic prosperity reach the poor, meeting basic needs (food, housing, education, health), and reducing inequality in wealth distribution. Land reforms and subsidies were key instruments. Despite growth, the gap between poor and rich widened -- green revolution exacerbated regional and farmer-size disparities.

nodes.label: Self-Help Groups (SHGs)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Since 1990s, beneficiaries encouraged to form SHGs. Members save and lend among themselves as small loans. Government provides partial financial assistance through banks, and SHGs decide loan allocation for self-employment activities. Under SGSY (Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana), this is the primary approach.

nodes.label: Critical Assessment of Poverty Programmes
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Three major problems: unequal land/asset distribution means benefits are captured by non-poor; resources allocated are insufficient compared to the magnitude of poverty; implementation depends on ill-motivated, inadequately trained, corruption-prone officials. No radical transformation in asset ownership or production processes achieved.

nodes.label: Rural vs Urban Poverty
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: More than 75% of India's poor reside in rural areas as landless agricultural labourers, small cultivators, or casual workers. Urban poor are largely overflow of rural poor migrating for employment. Poverty has been shifting from rural to urban areas over time. In 1990s, absolute rural poor declined but urban poor increased marginally.

nodes.label: Rural Development
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Comprehensive term focusing on development of lagging areas in village economy. Key areas: human resources (literacy, health), land reforms, productive resources, infrastructure (electricity, irrigation, credit, marketing, transport, roads), and poverty alleviation. Over two-thirds of India's population depends on agriculture, one-third of rural India in abject poverty.

nodes.label: Rural Credit System
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: At independence, moneylenders exploited farmers with high interest rates and manipulated accounts. After 1969 (social banking), multi-agency approach adopted. Institutional structure includes commercial banks, Regional Rural Banks (RRBs), cooperatives, and land development banks. Goal: adequate credit at cheaper rates for farmers with long gestation periods between sowing and income.

nodes.label: Critical Appraisal of Rural Banking
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Banking expansion helped post-green revolution farm output and food security. However, formal credit institutions chronically underperform. About 50% of defaulters are 'wilful defaulters'. Except commercial banks, institutions failed in deposit mobilisation and loan recovery. After reforms, rural banking expansion took a backseat.

nodes.label: Agricultural Marketing System
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Process involving assembling, storage, processing, transportation, packaging, grading, and distribution of agricultural commodities. Pre-independence: farmers suffered from faulty weighing, account manipulation, lack of price information, and storage. Even today, over 10% of farm produce wasted due to lack of storage. Government intervention through four measures.

nodes.label: Cooperative Marketing
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Third element of government marketing initiative. Success of milk cooperatives transformed Gujarat's social and economic landscape. However, cooperatives received setbacks due to inadequate farmer coverage, lack of marketing-processing links, and inefficient financial management.

nodes.label: Alternative Marketing Channels
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Direct farmer-to-consumer channels increasing farmer's share of consumer price. Examples: Apni Mandi (Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan), Hadaspar Mandi (Pune), Rythu Bazars (Andhra Pradesh), Uzhavar Sandies (Tamil Nadu). MNC food chains entering contracts/alliances with farmers for desired quality produce at pre-decided prices.

nodes.label: Organic Farming
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Whole system of farming that restores, maintains, and enhances ecological balance. Substitutes costly chemical inputs with locally produced organic inputs. Benefits: cheaper inputs, higher nutritional value, international export income, more employment (labour-intensive), pesticide-free produce. Limitations: lower initial yields, shorter shelf life, limited off-season crop choice.

nodes.label: IT in Rural Development
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: IT helps predict food insecurity, disseminates information on technologies, prices, weather, soil conditions. M.S. Swaminathan Research Foundation established Jamshedji Tata National Virtual Academy for Rural Prosperity providing info-kiosks. Government of India supported with Rs 100 crore. IT has potential for rural employment generation.

nodes.label: Worker-Population Ratio
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: About 40 per 100 persons are workers in India. Higher in rural areas (42) than urban (34) because rural people cannot afford to stay unemployed. For men: 52.7 overall; for women: 25.4 overall (29.9 rural, only 13.9 urban). Large gender gap in urban areas due to high male income discouraging female work and non-recognition of women's household work.
nodes.chapter_title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues

nodes.label: Jobless Growth
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: In the late 1990s, employment growth declined to levels of early planning stages while GDP grew positively. Widening gap between GDP growth and employment growth means India produces more goods and services without generating proportional employment. Employment grew at a stable 2% during 1960-2000 but decelerated in the late 1990s.
nodes.chapter_title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues

nodes.label: Casualisation of Workforce
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Over 1972-2000, proportion of self-employed declined from 61.4% to 52.6%, regular salaried from 15.4% to 14.6%, while casual wage labourers increased from 23.2% to 32.8%. This movement from self-employment and regular work to casual work makes workers highly vulnerable. A negative development in employment quality.
nodes.chapter_title: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues

nodes.label: Health Infrastructure in India
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Three-tier system: primary (PHC, CHC, sub-centres), secondary (district hospitals with surgery, X-ray, ECG), tertiary (advanced institutes like AIIMS). During 1951-2000: hospitals increased from 9,300 to 43,300, beds from 1.2 to 7.2 million. Eradicated smallpox, near-eradication of polio and leprosy. Less than 20% of population uses public health facilities.

nodes.label: Indian Systems of Medicine (AYUSH)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Six systems: Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Siddha, Naturopathy, and Homeopathy. India has 3,004 ISM hospitals, 23,028 dispensaries, and 6,11,431 registered practitioners. Has huge potential to solve healthcare problems being effective, safe, and inexpensive. But lacks framework for standardised education or research promotion.

nodes.label: Global Burden of Disease (GBD)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Measures premature death from diseases and years spent in disability. India has 17% of world population but bears 20% of global disease burden. Over half accounted by communicable diseases (diarrhoea, malaria, TB). About 5 lakh children die yearly of waterborne diseases. Malnutrition and inadequate vaccines kill 2.2 million children annually.

nodes.label: Air Pollution in India
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Widespread in urban areas with vehicles as major contributors. Motor vehicles increased from 3 lakh (1951) to 67 crores (2003). Personal transport (two-wheelers and cars) constitute 80% of registered vehicles. CPCB identified 17 categories of significantly polluting industries. Seventy per cent of India's water is polluted.

nodes.label: Ozone Depletion
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Reduction of ozone in stratosphere caused by chlorine and bromine compounds from CFCs (used in ACs, refrigerators) and halons (fire extinguishers). 5% reduction detected 1979-1990. Allows harmful UV radiation causing skin cancer, reducing phytoplankton. Led to Montreal Protocol banning CFCs and other ozone-depleting chemicals.

nodes.label: CNG in Urban Areas
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Compressed Natural Gas used as fuel in Delhi's public transport system. Has significantly lowered air pollution and made air cleaner in recent years. An example of a sustainable development strategy -- replacing polluting petrol/diesel with cleaner fuel in high-density urban areas.

nodes.label: Comparative Development: India, China, Pakistan
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: All three started developmental paths around the same time (India/Pakistan: 1947, China: 1949). Similar initial strategies: five year plans, large public sector, public expenditure on social development. Till 1980s, similar growth rates and per capita incomes. Diverged significantly after China's 1978 reforms and India's 1991 reforms.
nodes.chapter_title: Comparative Development Experiences of India and Its Neighbours

nodes.label: China's Development Path
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: After 1949, all critical sectors brought under government control. Great Leap Forward (1958) aimed at mass industrialisation. Communes for collective farming. Cultural Revolution (1966-76) sent students/professionals to countryside. 1978 reforms transformed economy: agriculture reform first, then industry. Present-day fast growth traces to 1978 reforms.
nodes.chapter_title: Comparative Development Experiences of India and Its Neighbours

nodes.label: Township and Village Enterprises (China)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Enterprises owned and operated by local collectives in China. Along with private sector firms, these were allowed to produce goods during the later phase of reforms. A distinctive feature of China's reform model -- decentralised, locally-owned enterprises that drove rural industrialisation.
nodes.chapter_title: Comparative Development Experiences of India and Its Neighbours

nodes.label: Pakistan's Development Path
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Follows mixed economy model like India. 1950s-60s: regulated policy framework with import substitution, tariff protection for consumer goods, direct import controls. 1970s: nationalisation of capital goods industries. Late 1970s-80s: denationalisation, private sector encouragement, Western financial support, and Middle East remittances. Reforms began 1988.
nodes.chapter_title: Comparative Development Experiences of India and Its Neighbours

nodes.label: Demographic Indicators Comparison
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: China is largest but has lowest density. Population growth highest in Pakistan, followed by India, then China. Sex ratio biased against females in all three due to son-preference. One of every six persons in the world is Indian, another is Chinese. Pakistan's population is roughly one-tenth of China or India.
nodes.chapter_title: Comparative Development Experiences of India and Its Neighbours

nodes.label: GDP and Economic Indicators Comparison
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: China leads in GDP, per capita GDP, and growth rates among the three. China's reform process since 1978 delivered faster growth than India's post-1991 reforms. India's GDP growth has accelerated but remains behind China. Pakistan's growth has been modest. All three share challenges of poverty, inequality, and need for structural transformation.
nodes.chapter_title: Comparative Development Experiences of India and Its Neighbours

nodes.label: Sectoral Contribution Comparison
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: In all three countries, agriculture's share of GDP has declined while industry and services have grown. China's industrial sector contribution is much higher than India's or Pakistan's. India's service sector growth is distinctive. All three started with agriculture-dominated economies but diverged in their structural transformation paths.
nodes.chapter_title: Comparative Development Experiences of India and Its Neighbours

nodes.label: India's Democratic Development Model
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: India, the world's largest democracy with a secular liberal Constitution, differs fundamentally from China's command economy (recently liberalising) and Pakistan's authoritarian militarist political structure. These political differences shaped economic policies and outcomes. India's mixed economy combined planning with private sector participation.
nodes.chapter_title: Comparative Development Experiences of India and Its Neighbours

nodes.label: Pakistan's Remittances and External Support
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: In the late 1970s and 1980s, Pakistan received financial support from Western nations and remittances from continuously increasing emigrant outflow to the Middle East. This stimulated economic growth alongside government incentives to the private sector, creating a conducive climate for new investments.
nodes.chapter_title: Comparative Development Experiences of India and Its Neighbours

nodes.label: Market Economy
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: An economic system where all economic activities are organized through the market via free interaction of individuals. Prices serve as signals for coordination -- when demand for a good rises, price rises, signaling producers to increase production. The USA is the closest example of a market economy.

nodes.label: Centrally Planned Economy
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: An economic system where the government or central authority plans all important economic activities -- production, exchange, and consumption decisions. Aims to achieve a desirable allocation of resources and equitable distribution. The Soviet Union was the closest historical example.

nodes.label: Price Mechanism
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The system by which prices of goods and services coordinate economic activities in a market economy. Prices send signals to producers and consumers -- a rising price signals higher demand, inducing increased supply. It is the 'invisible hand' (Adam Smith's concept) that brings coordination.

nodes.label: Microeconomics
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The branch of economics that studies the behaviour of individual economic agents -- consumers, firms, and markets for specific goods and services. Focuses on how prices and quantities are determined through interaction of individuals in individual markets.

nodes.label: Macroeconomics
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The branch of economics that studies the economy as a whole, focusing on aggregate measures such as total output (GDP), employment, aggregate price level, and national income. Examines how these aggregate measures are determined and change over time.

nodes.label: Resource Allocation
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The process of distributing scarce resources among competing uses to produce different goods and services. A particular allocation determines the mix of goods produced and their distribution among individuals. It is one of the central economic problems.

nodes.label: Factors of Production
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The inputs used in the production process: land, labour, capital, and entrepreneurship. These are the scarce resources that every economy must allocate among competing uses. Their prices (rent, wages, interest, profit) are determined in factor markets.

nodes.label: Economic Agents
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Decision-making units in an economy: households (consumers), firms (producers), and the government. Each agent makes decisions about production, consumption, and exchange. A decision-making unit can be a single person or a group like a household or firm.

nodes.label: Gross National Product (GNP)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The total market value of all final goods and services produced by nationals of a country, whether domestically or abroad. GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA). If NFIA is positive (nationals earn more abroad than foreigners earn domestically), GNP > GDP.

nodes.label: Net Domestic Product (NDP)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: GDP minus depreciation (consumption of fixed capital). NDP = GDP - Depreciation. NDP better reflects the net addition to the economy's productive capacity because it accounts for the wearing out of capital goods during production.

nodes.label: Net National Product (NNP)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: GNP minus depreciation. NNP = GNP - Depreciation. NNP at factor cost is called National Income -- it represents the total income earned by factors of production of a country. NNP at factor cost = NNP at market price - indirect taxes + subsidies.

nodes.label: Depreciation (Consumption of Fixed Capital)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The loss in value of fixed capital goods (machinery, equipment, buildings) due to normal wear and tear, obsolescence, or accidental damage during the production process. Deducting depreciation from gross measures gives net measures. Depreciation is not a part of factor income.

nodes.label: Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The difference between factor income earned by domestic residents abroad and factor income earned by foreign residents domestically. NFIA = Factor income earned abroad - Factor income paid to foreigners. GNP = GDP + NFIA. For India, NFIA is generally negative (foreigners earn more in India than Indians abroad).

nodes.label: Nominal GDP (GDP at Current Prices)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: GDP measured at the prevailing prices of the current year. Nominal GDP may increase due to actual increase in production OR merely due to rise in price level (inflation). Not suitable for comparing economic performance across years as it does not adjust for inflation.

nodes.label: Real GDP (GDP at Constant Prices)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: GDP measured at the prices of a base year, eliminating the effect of price changes. Better indicator of actual economic growth as it reflects changes in the quantity of goods and services produced. Real GDP growth rate measures true expansion of the economy.

nodes.label: Gross Investment (Gross Capital Formation)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Total expenditure on new capital goods (fixed capital like machinery and buildings) plus change in inventories (stocks). Gross Investment = Net Investment + Depreciation. Capital formation is necessary for economic growth. A high capital-output ratio means more capital is needed per unit of output.

nodes.label: Capital-Output Ratio
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The ratio of capital invested to the output produced. A high capital-output ratio means the economy needs more capital to produce each unit of output, indicating lower efficiency. Despite being a high-saving economy, India's growth has been limited by its high capital-output ratio.

nodes.label: Current Account
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Records trade in goods and services and transfer payments. Components: (1) Balance of trade (exports minus imports of goods), (2) Balance of invisibles (services, investment income, transfers including remittances). A current account deficit means the country imports more than it exports (spends more than it earns).

nodes.label: Balance of Trade (BoT)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: The difference between the value of exports and imports of goods (visible/merchandise trade). BoT = Exports - Imports. India typically has a trade deficit (imports exceed exports) driven by oil and gold imports. Trade deficit is a component of the current account.

nodes.label: Fixed Exchange Rate System
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: A system where the government or central bank fixes the exchange rate at a particular level. The central bank must buy or sell foreign currency to maintain the fixed rate. Requires large foreign exchange reserves. Devaluation is an official lowering of the fixed exchange rate by the government.

nodes.label: Flexible (Floating) Exchange Rate System
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: A system where the exchange rate is determined by market forces of demand and supply of foreign currency. The rate fluctuates freely. India follows a managed float system -- largely market-determined but RBI intervenes to prevent excessive volatility. Depreciation/appreciation occur through market forces.

nodes.label: Devaluation
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: An official reduction in the value of a country's currency under a fixed exchange rate system, decided by the government. Improves competitiveness of exports in foreign markets but makes imports costlier. Does NOT necessarily improve trade balance (depends on demand elasticities). India devalued the rupee in 1966 and 1991.

nodes.label: Currency Depreciation
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: A fall in the value of a currency caused by market forces under a floating exchange rate system. When the rupee depreciates, RBI may sell dollars to arrest the slide. Measures to prevent slide include: curbing non-essential imports, encouraging Masala Bonds, easing ECB conditions. Expansionary monetary policy would NOT help.

nodes.label: Currency Appreciation
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: A rise in the value of a currency due to market forces under a floating exchange rate. Makes exports costlier and imports cheaper. An increase in NEER (Nominal Effective Exchange Rate) indicates appreciation. Appreciation may hurt export competitiveness.

nodes.label: Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: A weighted average of bilateral exchange rates of the domestic currency vis-a-vis a basket of foreign currencies. An increase in NEER indicates appreciation of the domestic currency. NEER does not adjust for inflation differences between countries.

nodes.label: External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Loans raised by Indian entities from foreign sources. When the rupee depreciates, the effective cost of servicing ECBs increases (currency risk). Devaluation of domestic currency does NOT decrease the currency risk of ECBs -- it increases it. Capital flight due to US Fed rate hikes can also increase ECB costs.

nodes.label: Remittances
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Money sent by Indians living and working abroad back to India. Recorded as transfer payments in the current account. India is the world's largest recipient of remittances. Along with IT sector earnings, remittances help reduce the risk of a currency crisis by providing stable foreign exchange inflows.

nodes.label: Land (Factor of Production)
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: A natural resource and fixed factor of production. Cultivated area in India has remained largely stable at around 140-155 million hectares since 1970. Less than 40% of total cultivated area is irrigated.

nodes.label: Physical Capital
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Divided into fixed capital (tools, machines, buildings -- used over many years) and working capital (raw materials, money in hand -- used up in production). Modern farming requires substantially more physical capital than traditional methods.

nodes.label: Fixed Capital
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Tools, machines, and buildings that can be used in production over many years. Examples: tractors, tubewells, threshers. Distinguished from working capital which is consumed during production.

nodes.label: Working Capital
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Raw materials and money in hand that are used up during production. Includes seeds, fertilisers, pesticides, yarn, clay. Unlike fixed capital, these are consumed in a single production cycle.

nodes.label: Non-Farm Activities
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Activities other than farming: dairy, small-scale manufacturing, transport, shopkeeping. Only 25% of rural workers engaged in non-farm sector. Require little land but need capital and access to markets. Key for rural employment diversification.

nodes.label: Modern Farming Methods
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Use of HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, pesticides, tubewells, and farm machinery (tractors, threshers). Requires more cash/capital than traditional farming. Led to higher yields but also environmental degradation -- soil fertility loss and groundwater depletion.

nodes.label: Irrigation System
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Electricity-powered tubewells transformed farming by enabling irrigation of entire cultivated area. Persian wheels replaced by tubewells. By mid-1970s, 200 hectares in Palampur fully irrigated. Less than 40% of India's cultivated land is irrigated.

nodes.label: Small Farmers and Credit
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Small farmers must borrow for working capital from large farmers, moneylenders, or traders at very high interest rates (e.g., 24% for 4 months). They lack savings from surplus. Indebtedness is both cause and effect of poverty among small farmers.

nodes.label: Food Security
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Ensured when all people at all times have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food. Three dimensions: availability (production + imports + stocks), accessibility (within reach), and affordability (enough money to buy). Amartya Sen emphasised 'entitlements' approach.

nodes.label: Ration Cards
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Three types: (a) Antyodaya cards for poorest of the poor, (b) BPL cards for those below poverty line, (c) APL cards for all others. Each card entitles family to buy stipulated quantity (e.g., 35 kg grains, 5 litres kerosene, 5 kg sugar) monthly from ration shops.

nodes.label: Cooperatives in Food Security
nodes.subject: economics
nodes.detail: Important role especially in southern and western India. Tamil Nadu: 94% of fair price shops run by cooperatives. Mother Dairy (Delhi): milk and vegetables at controlled rates. Amul (Gujarat): White Revolution success story. ADS (Maharashtra): grain banks for food security.
